Local search decides who gets the booking

The unglamorous work carries this: a complete and actively maintained Google Business Profile, categories that match how people actually search, service attributes filled in, real photography rather than stock, and name, address and phone details identical everywhere they appear. Conflicting details across directories and aggregators are the single most common reason a well-reviewed restaurant underperforms in maps.

Your menu is data, not decoration

A menu published as a PDF or a flat image is invisible to every system that matters. It cannot be parsed, cannot be quoted, and cannot answer a constrained question like “vegan mains under £15 near me”.

Marked up properly, the same menu becomes an answer. Dish names, prices, cuisine, and dietary attributes such as halal, vegan and gluten-free stop being marketing copy and start being retrievable facts. Combined with Restaurant, Menu and OpeningHoursSpecification schema, that data is what an assistant repeats back to a hungry buyer. Anything you leave unmarked is left to inference, and inference favours whoever documented themselves better.

Reviews are the ranking signal you cannot write yourself

Rating and review volume feed both map rankings and the trust layer that generative engines lean on. What matters is not a one-off push to hit a number, but velocity and recency — a steady flow of recent, specific reviews beats a large pile of old ones.

I set up the asking mechanics so requests land at the moment the guest is happiest, then make sure responses are handled properly. Replying to criticism in public, calmly and specifically, converts better than any five-star average, because prospective guests read how you handle problems.

The queries that actually decide the deal

Bottom-of-funnel intent in SaaS lives outside your brand. It looks like best [category] software, [competitor] alternatives, [you] vs [competitor], [category] for [role or industry], pricing questions and integration questions.

Each of those needs its own page with its own angle. A single features page cannot serve six different intents, and trying to make it do so is the most common reason technically strong products stay invisible. Comparison and alternative pages in particular feel uncomfortable to write because they name competitors — which is precisely why they convert and why they get cited.

Page architecture that scales without turning into sprawl

The architecture I build for software companies runs on four families: feature pages covering what the product does, use-case pages covering who it is for, integration pages covering what it connects to, and comparison pages covering why you over the alternatives.

Each family targets a different stage of the decision, and each adds entities that strengthen the others. Done properly this compounds; done carelessly it becomes hundreds of thin, templated pages that dilute the site. The dividing line is whether each page answers a question a real buyer asked, in language they used.

Documentation and changelogs are search assets

Most technology companies treat docs as a support cost. In practice, documentation is often the most linked, most cited and most specific content the company owns — developers search error messages, API methods and configuration questions constantly.

If your docs sit behind JavaScript, on a subdomain nobody links to, or in a tool that blocks crawlers, you are discarding your strongest technical authority signal. Making them crawlable, well-structured and internally linked is usually one of the highest-return technical fixes available, and it sits squarely inside technical SEO.

Third-party platforms decide part of your visibility

For software, review platforms and roundups occupy a large share of the results your buyers see. G2, Capterra, industry roundups and community threads frequently outrank vendor sites for category queries, and they are heavily used as sources by generative engines because they read as independent consensus.

You cannot rank a listing you do not own, but you can influence it: keep your category placement and product descriptions accurate, maintain review flow, and make sure the facts on those profiles match your own site exactly. Contradictions between your pricing page and your G2 profile are a trust problem before they are a ranking problem.

Getting recommended inside AI answers

Software evaluation is one of the fastest-moving categories for AI-assisted research. Buyers ask assistants to compare tools, summarise pricing models and recommend options for a stated constraint — team size, budget, compliance requirement, existing stack.

Being included in those answers depends on the same discipline as AEO and GEO anywhere else: state facts explicitly rather than implying them, structure pages so passages can be extracted cleanly, mark up SoftwareApplication and offer data, and ensure independent sources corroborate what you claim. Vague positioning language is invisible to a retrieval system.

Sessions are a poor proxy for a business that sells subscriptions. I report on qualified signups and trials from organic, assisted conversions across the longer research path, and share of visibility on the specific comparison and category queries that precede a purchase.

I also run a fixed panel of buying prompts through the major assistants each month and log whether the product is mentioned and how it is described. When a model gets your pricing model or integration list wrong, that is a content gap you can fix — and it is usually costing you deals silently.

I map the category, find which decision-stage queries have no page behind them, fix the technical issues blocking crawl and render, then build the missing pages in order of commercial value. Category pages earn the rankings, product pages close the sale

A category page that ranks needs a reason to exist beyond listing products: buying guidance, the distinctions that matter in that category, the questions people ask before choosing. That content also feeds answer engines, which quote explanation far more readily than a product grid.

Faceted navigation is where crawl budget goes to die

Filters are the single most destructive pattern in retail SEO. Four filters with five options each generate hundreds of combinations, and if every combination is crawlable you have quietly created more URLs than you have products.

The decision is per-parameter, not global. Facets with genuine search demand and unique inventory — brand, size, colour, material — deserve indexable, linkable URLs with their own titles. Facets that only reorder the same items — sort order, page size, session identifiers, arbitrary price bands — should never be indexable. Product data has to be complete, not just present

Marking up a product with a name and an image is close to useless. The fields that decide whether you appear in a rich result or a generated comparison are the commercial ones: price, availability, aggregateRating, gtin, shipping details and return policy.

A feed that says in stock while the page says sold out is a trust problem, and it is the kind of inconsistency that quietly removes a store from consideration.

Out-of-stock and discontinued products

Retail sites accumulate dead URLs faster than any other type. The instinct is to delete them in bulk, which throws away every link and ranking signal those pages earned.

Seasonal products that will return should stay live with clear availability status. Permanently discontinued items should redirect to the closest equivalent or the parent category — never to the homepage, which search engines treat as a soft 404. Handled well, a retired product keeps working for you; handled badly, it is a slow leak.

Reviews and user-generated content

Reviews do three jobs at once in retail: they corroborate your claims, they cover long-tail phrasing you would never think to target, and they keep product pages fresh without anyone writing anything. Questions and answers on product pages do the same, and often answer the exact objection blocking the sale.

Collect them honestly and mark them up accurately. Review markup that does not match visible reviews is a shortcut that ends badly.

SEO, AEO and GEO Services for Finance and Insurance

Financial content is evaluated more strictly than almost anything else on the web. It is squarely “Your Money or Your Life”, it is regulated, and the search results are dominated by comparison sites and institutions with enormous authority. Publishing something generic here is not just ineffective, it is a liability.

The firms that win are the ones prepared to be precise, dated, attributed and honest about limits — which happens to be the same thing regulators want.

Accuracy is the ranking strategy

Financial figures decay. Rates change, thresholds move, allowances are revised, products get withdrawn. An article quoting last year's numbers with no date on it is worse than no article, because it actively misleads and signals neglect.

Everything numerical needs a visible date, a source and a review cycle. I build that maintenance schedule into the content plan rather than treating it as an afterthought, because in finance freshness is not a vanity signal — it is the difference between being useful and being wrong.

Attribution and regulatory clarity

Every substantive page should carry a named author with relevant qualifications, the firm's regulatory registration, and an unambiguous statement of whether the content is guidance or advice. That distinction matters legally and it matters to the reader.

Risk warnings, conflicts of interest and commission arrangements should be stated plainly rather than buried. Counter-intuitively, disclosure builds the trust that converts, and it provides exactly the signals that quality evaluation looks for.

Comparison and calculator pages

The most valuable finance pages are functional. A calculator that shows its workings, a comparison table that admits where a product is not the best fit, an eligibility checker that gives a straight answer — these earn links, get cited, and convert because they are genuinely useful.

What does not work is the thin product summary that restates a provider's marketing. Comparison sites already own that ground with more data and more authority.

Long-tail questions are where the room is

You will not outrank a major comparison site for a head term, and chasing it wastes budget. The winnable ground is the specific, awkward, situational question: what happens to a policy in a particular circumstance, how a rule applies to an unusual case, what to do when something goes wrong.

These queries have lower volume and dramatically higher intent, they are poorly served, and they are exactly what people now ask assistants in full sentences.

Getting cited without overstating

Assistants are deliberately conservative with financial questions and prefer sources that are clearly attributed, dated and hedged appropriately. Content that guarantees returns or promises approval is filtered out precisely because it reads as unreliable.

Structure the answer directly under a question-shaped heading, keep claims verifiable, and mark up organisation and author properly. This is the same method as my AEO and GEO work, applied where the evidence bar is highest.

Local and adviser-level visibility

Much advisory business is still won locally and personally. Individual adviser profiles, branch pages and consistent details across directories capture demand that the corporate brand page never will — people search for the adviser they were recommended, by name. The structural side sits in my local SEO services.

Technical trust signals

In finance the basics carry unusual weight. Secure delivery, fast pages, clear contact routes, a visible complaints procedure and accessible forms all contribute to whether a visitor believes the firm is legitimate. Users are actively scanning for reasons to distrust a financial site, and slow or broken experiences supply them.

Measuring in a regulated funnel

Lead volume alone is misleading when many enquiries will not qualify. I report on qualified enquiries after eligibility filtering, assisted conversions across a long consideration path, and visibility on the situational queries that indicate genuine intent — alongside a monthly check on how assistants describe the firm and its products.

Content that survives a compliance review

The fastest way to stall a finance content programme is to write it first and send it to compliance afterwards. Everything comes back marked up, deadlines slip, and the team stops publishing.

I work the other way round: agree the claim boundaries, the required disclosures and the approved phrasing up front, then write inside them. It is far quicker, and the resulting content is usually better, because being forced to state exactly what you can support removes the vague marketing language that was never going to rank anyway.

With accuracy and attribution, because they are both the compliance requirement and the ranking constraint. Then the functional pages worth building, then the long-tail question set. A free SEO audit will show which of your figures are undated and which questions you are absent from.

Travel is the most seasonal, most inspiration-led and most competitive consumer vertical in search. The decision starts months before any money is spent, moves through several distinct phases, and is contested by OTAs, review platforms and publishers with enormous authority.

Most travel operators publish only for the final phase — availability and price — and then wonder why the audience arrives already committed to someone else.

Four phases, four kinds of content

Travel search moves through dreaming, planning, booking and being there. Each phase has a different query shape and needs a different page.

Dreaming is destination guides and “best time to visit”. Planning is itineraries, where to stay and budgets. Booking is availability, price and cancellation terms. In-destination is “near me”, opening hours and practical detail on a phone with poor signal. Publishing only for booking means competing at the most expensive moment against everyone else, having contributed nothing earlier.

Guides earn the audience; booking pages convert it

Destination and itinerary content is what earns links, gets shared and gets quoted by assistants. It rarely converts directly, which is why it is often cut — and why the operators who keep investing in it end up owning the audience.

Written well, a guide answers the questions a first-time visitor actually has: how long to spend, what is genuinely worth it, what to skip, how to get between places, what it costs. Generic destination copy assembled from other websites achieves none of this.

Seasonality has to be planned backwards

The most common mistake in travel SEO is publishing seasonal content during the season. By then the ranking window has closed — the people booking summer travel were searching in winter.

Content for a peak needs to exist and be indexed months ahead, then be refreshed rather than replaced each year so it accumulates authority instead of restarting. That single change in timing often matters more than the content itself.

Practical detail is a ranking asset

Opening hours, ticket prices, transport connections, accessibility, whether somewhere takes cards — these unglamorous specifics are what in-destination searchers need and what assistants quote most readily.

They also date quickly, so they need an owner and a review cycle. A guide with last year's prices erodes the trust the rest of the content built.

Competing with OTAs and review platforms

You will not outrank the major booking platforms on transactional terms, and you should not spend trying. What you can own is genuine first-hand local knowledge, which aggregators cannot manufacture and models increasingly prefer.

Direct bookings are also worth substantially more than commissioned ones, so content that builds enough trust to bypass the platform pays twice.

Being recommended by assistants

Trip planning suits conversational tools unusually well — people describe a budget, a duration, who they are travelling with and what they enjoy, and ask for a plan. Those answers are built from sources with specific, structured, current information.

Being included means stating facts plainly, structuring itineraries so they can be extracted, and keeping details accurate. This is my AEO and GEO method applied to a vertical where it is unusually effective.

Local visibility in-destination

For anything with a physical location — a hotel, tour operator, attraction or restaurant — the local layer decides in-destination discovery. Accurate hours, seasonal opening changes and a maintained profile matter more than any page, and are covered by my local SEO services.

Measuring a long, multi-touch journey

A traveller may read a guide in January and book in April through a branded search. Last-click reporting will credit the brand and value the guide at zero.

I report on assisted conversions across the whole path, on direct versus commissioned bookings, and on visibility across all four phases rather than only the transactional one.

Photography, video and page weight

Travel sells visually, so these sites carry heavy imagery — and they are frequently browsed on mobile data, sometimes abroad on a poor connection. Page weight is a conversion problem here in a way it is not elsewhere.

Modern formats, genuine lazy loading and correctly sized images usually take several seconds off a gallery page without touching how it looks. For in-destination searches, where someone is standing on a street trying to check your opening hours, that difference decides whether they wait or go elsewhere.

Industrial buyers are the most specific searchers on the internet. An engineer looking for a component searches a material, a tolerance, a standard or a part number — not a slogan. If your site cannot answer at that level of precision, you are not in the consideration set, no matter how good the factory is.

Manufacturing is also the sector where the most valuable information is routinely locked away in PDFs, behind forms, or in a catalogue nobody can crawl.

Specifications belong in HTML

The single most damaging pattern in industrial SEO is the PDF-only catalogue. Everything a buyer needs — dimensions, tolerances, materials, load ratings, compliance — sits inside a download, often gated behind a form.

That content cannot be crawled properly, cannot be quoted by an assistant, and gives each product no individual URL to rank. Specifications need to be in HTML tables on a page per product line, with the PDF offered as an extra rather than as the only source. This one change frequently transforms visibility for manufacturers who have never ranked for anything but their company name.

Buyers search capability, not just product

Alongside product searches, industrial buyers search for what you can do: a process, a volume range, a material, a lead time, a certification. “CNC machining for aerospace, low volume” is a capability query, and it needs a capability page.

Those pages are usually missing entirely, or compressed into a single “what we do” page that matches nothing specifically. Building one page per meaningful capability, with real parameters rather than adjectives, captures demand competitors are not even contesting.

Certification is a filter, not a footnote

In regulated and safety-critical supply chains, certification is a hard filter. A buyer who needs a specific standard will exclude every supplier who does not state it clearly, before comparing anything else.

Standards, approvals, test reports and traceability should be stated in text on relevant pages, not shown as a row of logos in a footer. A logo image is invisible to a language model summarising your capabilities.

Long, technical sales cycles need patient content

An industrial purchase can involve several people over many months — an engineer specifying, a buyer negotiating, a manager approving. Each searches differently and needs different material.

Technical documentation serves the engineer, capability and capacity pages serve the buyer, and case evidence and certification serve the approver. Sites built only for one of the three stall at the other two.

The RFQ is your conversion event

Most manufacturing sites treat the enquiry form as an afterthought. If a buyer has to guess what information you need, or fill in fifteen fields to ask one question, they will contact whoever made it easier.

State minimum order quantities, sample policy, typical lead times and who the enquiry reaches. Pre-qualifying honestly reduces wasted quoting and increases genuine RFQs.

Being retrieved by assistants

Procurement research has moved into conversational tools quickly, because comparing suppliers on stated parameters is exactly what they are good at. A buyer describes a requirement and asks which suppliers can meet it. 

Only suppliers whose capabilities, tolerances and certifications exist as machine-readable text qualify. My AEO and GEO work makes those parameters explicit, and technical SEO makes sure the pages holding them can actually be fetched and rendered.

Measuring a low-volume, high-value funnel

A manufacturer may need twelve good RFQs a year, not twelve thousand visitors. Traffic reporting is close to meaningless at that scale.

I report on RFQs and sample requests, which capability or specification pages produced them, and visibility on the parameter-level queries your best customers use. Where a CRM exists, I connect enquiries back to the page that generated them so you can see which specifications are worth expanding.

Distributors and large catalogues

Distributors face the same problem multiplied. Thousands of lines, often supplied as a manufacturer feed, frequently published as near-identical pages that compete with each other and with the manufacturer's own site.

The answer is not to publish every line as a thin page. It is to build genuine depth where you have demand or margin, group the rest into well-structured category pages, and add something the manufacturer does not offer — stock position, local lead time, application guidance or compatibility detail. Without that, you are asking a search engine to prefer your copy of a datasheet over the original.

By getting specifications out of PDFs and into crawlable pages, because that is almost always the largest single constraint. Then capability pages, then certification clarity and the RFQ path. A free SEO audit will show how much of your catalogue is currently invisible.
